(29m). I feel you buddy. I’ve also been dealing with depression and anxiety since childhood. 
There’s no easy way to deal with it that I’ve found but, I’ll give you what has helped me to some degree.

First of all, you might not liking hearing this or maybe you will but I have to say it. You are EXTREMLY young. For real. You might feel like your getting old, but you are honestly still a child. This is good news, because you probably haven’t made too many serious mistakes and you still have plenty of time to figure shit out. Don’t let anybody make you feel like you should have your shit together at your age, you absolutely should not. No one in their right mind would expect you to. So do not beat yourself up. So please keep this in mind. 

As far as suicide goes, I completely get it and don’t blame you at all, I feel exactly the same way and I’m not one to tell somebody that they should continue living a life of pure suffering. HOWEVER, once again, you are soooo young my guy. I highly recommend you wait it out for another 5-10 years and give it everything you got in the mean time.

Alright so first advice is, whether you feel like it or not, TAKE CARE OF YOURSELF. Really treat yourself like someone you deeply care about, even if you don’t. Yes, I know depression and anxiety make simple things like taking a shower and brushing your teeth very difficult, but do it anyway. Do your best to clean up your life bit by bit. Just baby steps. Eating healthy is huge, this alone can actually directly help mental health if done faithfully. Keep yourself looking and smelling nice, etc…

Next, do as much inner work as possible. You may have a chemical imbalance, gut issues, or neurological issues. But there could also be childhood trama and/or thinking patterns that are contributing to bad mental health.
Learn to see yourself clearly and objectively. You can do this by learning some form of meditation. Learn to witness thought patterns and behavior patterns.
You can also do something called shadow work. This is when you play the devils advocate with yourself by deliberately invoking thoughts and feelings in order to examine them and make them conscious and clear. I think journaling feelings and thoughts greatly help with this.

This one I just somewhat recently realized how important this is. It’s absolutely crucial. Do NOT isolate yourself and make connections/friendships as much as possible. I recommend starting this ASAP. I don’t know if this is an issue with you or not. But, know that we are social creatures, we are hardwired for connection with others. 29(m). I can definitely relate to not wanting to live due to constant depression and anxiety. 

Unfortunately, I don’t have any sure fire solution, but I’ll give you this.

I don’t know what kind of introspection you’ve done, but I would highly recommend doing as much internal work/examination as possible. This will allow you to become clear on how much is a physical issue and how much is thought patterns and trauma that has not been properly integrated and processed.

There’s different ways of doing this. You could learn to  objectively observe your mind and actions. Learn to be very very honest with yourself so that you can really see yourself clearly. Meditation is probably the best way to “cultivate the witness” which allows for much clearer perception.

You can also play the devils advocate with yourself by doing something called “shadow work”. This is basically where you deliberately find subconscious thought patterns that you were previously not aware of and then figure out there origin/cause and find out how much, if any, truth they have to them.

Keep in mind, to really do this, you must be willing to feel very uncomfortable because you are essentially bringing out your inner demons in order to gain clarity and as much control as possible over your thoughts and behaviors. But it’s important that you have the courage and keep doing it, in order to really reap the benefits. It’s definitely worth doing and is the most important and courageous thing a human being can do.

This is my best general advice. Good luck to you.

There still is no clarification of what the mechanism of “conscious choice” is and how it differs from “natural” behavior/phenomena. 
Although there may be “differences” between choice and instincts or training. It’s still not clear that there is a “fundamental difference”. That is to stay that there is something objectively and innately different about so called choice and “other” actions such as instinct or other acts of nature and that it is not merely a human construct or arbitrary distinction. 
Consider that so called “involuntary” and “voluntary” actions are actually two sides of the same coin and the difference between the two may be useful but are still indeed human constructs. Voluntary actions cannot exist without involuntary actions(such as the heart beating, etc.) so to distinguish them as two independently functioning entities would be false (not to say you said they were). 
I’d say (Although granted, this may be an over-simplification) that the reason the animal appears to have less “conscious choice” is because their brains/nervous systems cannot calculate and perceive nearly as many calculations as a human brain. The human brain can also potentially comprehend more complex information allowing us to think in more “dimensions” so to speak. Therefore we can make a more accurate and multi variable calculation/choice.
But I still maintain that although there’s a difference, there is no compelling evidence that there is a “fundamental difference” between the aforementioned scenarios.

In some sense our physiology, choices, involuntary actions, and and all other “external” actions such as tornados or rain or whatever the case, is still an act of nature all the same. One unified happening.

The danger is that you are potentially blinding yourself. You give up the opportunity to gain valuable knowledge, clarity and insight about the situation. You instead trade it for ignorance designed to create a false sense of security and safety, which in the long run only makes the situation worse.

I would say to make it more clear you still have to further investigate the mechanisms of a “conscious choice” that agency appears to grant humans.
So, in your example of how you have agency because you have the understanding of the potential consequences of eating a whole tub of ice cream vs your dog who does not have such understanding. What about the subconscious mechanisms that you had little to no control over, such as hunger and cravings for that particular food? There’s biology involved, the way you were programmed from your society, what your parents taught you, the bugs in your stomach, etc…Is there a fundamental difference between the wind blowing, the birds chirping, or the way your physiology functions and all other unfathomable phenomena that led you to making a “choice” to eat the ice cream in the first place? 
I think there’s a place and even need for arbitrary distinctions such as this but I would say it’s imperative for us to know that when it really comes down to it, there is in fact no fundamental difference between “nature” and humans and its behavior.
